rv.q: Midnight Movie is funny, engaging and, on its own terms, wholly successful.
By the end, it coalesces into a highly imaginative theatrical experience even if all the online flitting brings a degree of weariness, just as it does in life.
Although it's a bold, occasionally brilliant play, waiting for the narrative to cohere does feel a bit like staring at a spinny wheel of death as a page tries to load.

Its attempts to unpack the pleasures and dangers of digital voyeurism and society's social media obsession are unremarkable, but Midnight Movie succeeds in its ambitious attempt to appeal to underrepresented audiences.
A bold experiment in which the results prove less intriguing than the premise.
I was left a bit bewildered and even bored by this 75-minute affair, at moments craving a quiet night in on the sofa with glass of red wine in hand.
Rachel Bagshaw's production is a slick, spirited and tech-heavy 70 minutes... staging feels formless for just that moment too long though – dragging when it could be disorientingly delightful.'

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this inventive exploration of chronic pain and digital escape, praising Eve Leigh's creative concept and visual flair, though some find the high-concept approach more elliptical than engaging.
